```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "omip43")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/06_omip43_asc_analysis.R first."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}
```

## Why this dataset

OMIP-043 identifies antibody secreting cells, historically called plasma cells,
across four human tissues [1]. Its target population is defined as CD38 high and
CD27 positive, and that word "high" turns out to decide everything that follows.
CD38 high is the bright end of one continuous distribution rather than a separated
peak, so a method that looks for a dip between two peaks has to be checked rather
than trusted.

The dataset is also unusually good for checking arithmetic. The authors state
their design target in counting terms, and both halves of that sentence can be
tested against the data they deposited.

The aim is to reproduce the paper's findings as closely as the deposited data
allows. The report works through the manual gates, the counting claims, automated
gating and how it behaves, the evidence for why it behaves that way, clustering,
the phenotype claims, and finally a verdict on every claim in one table.

### What the replicates are

Each tissue group holds seven files that share one `$SRC` and one acquisition
date of 3 August 2017. They are replicate acquisitions of one preparation per
tissue, not seven donors.

That is the useful case here. Donor variation is absent by construction, so the
spread across the seven measures acquisition and analysis and nothing else. It is
the Maecker design in miniature, on one bench instead of fifteen laboratories.

## Part 1: the manual gates

The deposited workspace gates seven populations in sequence: a time gate, a
viability gate, a permissive scatter gate, two singlet gates, a dump gate for
CD3, CD14, CD15 and CD193, and finally the ASC gate.

```{r}
#| label: manual-counts

manual <- ReadOutput("manual_asc_counts.csv")
kable(
  manual[, c("tissue", "parent_events", "asc_events", "asc_percent",
             "poisson_cv_percent")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Every replicate. The parent is the dumped population, which is what the paper uses as its denominator.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Parent events", "ASC events", "ASC percent",
                "Poisson CV percent")
)
```

The frequencies span an order of magnitude between tissues, from 0.23 percent in
blood to 3.5 percent in spleen. Within a tissue the seven replicates agree
closely, which is what replicate acquisitions of one tube should do.

## Part 2: the counting claims

The paper states its design target directly:

> We targeted a 5% coefficient of variation (CV), which resulted in regularly
> collecting 400-2,000 events in the ASC gate.

Those two numbers are one claim, because they are related by arithmetic. A count
of rare events follows a Poisson distribution, so the relative spread from
counting alone is `1 / sqrt(n)`. At 400 events that is exactly 5 percent, which is
where the paper's lower bound comes from.

```{r}
#| label: counting-claims

counting <- ReadOutput("counting_claims.csv")
kable(
  counting,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The paper's two targets, checked against its own data.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Mean events", "All in 400 to 2000",
                "Replicates in range", "Poisson CV percent", "Meets 5 percent CV")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: count-plot
#| fig-cap: "Events in the ASC gate. The band is the paper's stated range."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("asc_event_counts.png"))
```

Not one of the 28 replicates falls inside the stated 400 to 2,000 range. Blood
and bone marrow sit below it at 290 and 185 events, and spleen and tonsil sit
above it at around 3,500.

That is worth stating carefully, because it is not an error in the paper. The
sentence says "regularly", which is a description of the authors' usual practice
across many experiments rather than a promise about this particular deposit. The
5 percent CV target is met where the count is high enough, in spleen and tonsil,
and missed in blood and bone marrow where the cells are rarest. The target
describes an aim; this deposit shows where the aim is hard to reach.

### The floor and what sits above it

The Poisson CV is a floor. No amount of care in the laboratory goes below it,
because it is the spread of the counting itself. The measured CV across the seven
replicates includes that floor plus pipetting, staining, acquisition and the gate.

```{r}
#| label: spread

spread <- ReadOutput("asc_spread.csv")
kable(
  spread,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The counting floor against what seven replicates actually did.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Replicates", "Mean count", "Mean percent",
                "Poisson CV percent", "Measured CV percent", "Excess CV percent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: cv-plot
#| fig-cap: "The two coefficients of variation, by tissue."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cv_comparison.png"))
```

Read the last column. In blood, bone marrow and spleen the measured spread sits
above the counting floor, so something other than counting is contributing. In
tonsil the measured CV of 1.17 percent falls below the Poisson floor of 1.73
percent, and the excess is reported as missing rather than as a negative number.

A measured spread below the counting floor is not possible for independent
samples. It means the seven tonsil files are not independent, which fits what they
are: repeated acquisitions from one tube, where the same cells can be sampled more
than once and the counts are correlated. The arithmetic detected the study design.

## Part 3: automated gating, and why it fails

The template mirrors the manual hierarchy, with `mindensity` for the viability and
dump gates and two sequential `mindensity` gates to reach CD38 high.

```{r}
#| label: template

template <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip43_gating_template.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  template[, c("alias", "pop", "parent", "dims", "gating_method", "gating_args")],
  caption = "The template. It runs without error and the answer is wrong."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: automated

automated <- ReadOutput("automated_vs_manual.csv")
kable(
  automated[, c("tissue", "asc_percent_manual", "asc_percent_automated",
                "fold_error")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The template against the manual mean, one replicate per tissue.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Manual percent", "Automated percent", "Fold error")
)
```

This is worse than a wrong answer. The template is wrong in both directions and by
a different amount in each tissue: it undercounts bone marrow threefold and
overcounts spleen eighteenfold. A method that is consistently wrong can be
corrected. A method whose error changes sign between tissues cannot be trusted
anywhere.

### What the gate is, read from the workspace

The manual ASC gate is a `rectangleGate` on CD38 from 141.8 to 209.1 and CD27 from
109.7 to 211.3. A human placed a box, using knowledge of where these cells sit.
That is a threshold decision and not a boundary the data announces.

The paper says as much in its own words:

> On-scale display of CD38high events is critical for ASC identification, and can
> be difficult for the untrained eye.

## Part 3b: where a density method actually cuts

The section above shows that the template is wrong. It does not show why, and the
obvious explanation is worth testing rather than asserting.

`mindensity` was therefore run on the CD38 channel of exactly the data the analyst
looked at, in the workspace's own scale, and its threshold compared with theirs.

```{r}
#| label: cd38-thresholds

thresholds <- ReadOutput("cd38_thresholds.csv")
kable(
  thresholds,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Where each method cuts CD38, on the same events, in the same scale.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Analyst threshold", "mindensity threshold",
                "Percent above analyst", "Percent above mindensity",
                "Manual ASC percent")
)
```

This corrects the simple story. In spleen the two methods almost agree: 144.2
against 141.8, giving 3.48 percent of events above the cut against 3.59 percent.
A single density gate on CD38 would have been close to right there.

In the other three tissues `mindensity` cuts far too low, at 80, 73 and 84 against
analyst thresholds of 124, 128 and 142. It keeps 27, 35 and 14 percent of events
where the analyst kept 3.1, 0.8 and 0.9 percent.

So the method is not blind. It succeeds where the target population is abundant
enough to bend the density curve, which in spleen means 3.3 percent of events, and
fails where the population is rare, which in the other three tissues means 0.3 to
0.9 percent. The rarer the cell, the less of a feature it leaves for a density
method to find, and this is a rare cell panel.

```{r}
#| label: cd38-density
#| fig-cap: "Spleen. The solid line is the analyst's threshold, the dashed line is where mindensity cuts."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd38_density.png"))
```

The figure shows what the arithmetic says. There is one large mode and a long
shoulder, and `mindensity` finds the dip between negative and positive rather than
the start of the bright tail.

```{r}
#| label: cd38-biaxial
#| fig-cap: "The plot the analyst drew on. The red box is their gate, the dashed line is the density cut."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd38_cd27_biaxial.png"))
```

Note also that the analyst's gate has an upper bound on both markers. A density
threshold has no upper bound at all, so even where the lower edges agree the two
gates are not the same object.

## Part 4: clustering recovers what gating missed

Clustering does not need a valley. It groups events by their position in all seven
markers at once, and ASC differ from everything around them on several of those
markers together: CD38 bright, CD27 positive, CD20 low and side scatter high.

The manual gate is used here only to score the result. The clustering never sees
it.

```{r}
#| label: clustering

clustering <- ReadOutput("clustering_summary.csv")
kable(
  clustering,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "FlowSOM with 15 metaclusters, scored against the manual ASC gate.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Manual ASC", "Manual percent", "Best cluster purity",
                "Best cluster recall", "ASC clusters", "Combined recall",
                "Combined percent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-manual
#| fig-cap: "Spleen. Red is the ASC gate the authors drew. The embedding was built without it."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_spleen_manual.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-clusters
#| fig-cap: "The same embedding, coloured by metacluster."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_spleen_clusters.png"))
```

In three of the four tissues a single metacluster is over 91 percent ASC. Recall
runs from 72 to 95 percent, and in spleen a second cluster takes the combined
recall to 97.4 percent.

Blood is the weakest case at 63.2 percent purity, and that is expected. With 165
ASC among 50,000 events, the population is too small to hold a metacluster of its
own and it shares one with its nearest neighbours.

### How each metacluster was labelled

Purity and recall say whether a cluster matches the manual gate. They do not say
what any cluster is. FlowSOM returns fifteen numbered groups and nothing else.

No cluster was named by eye. The rule is in a file and it runs in four steps.

**Step 1. Write down what each cell type looks like.** The definitions file gives
the expected sign of each marker for each type, as `pos`, `neg`, `high`, or blank
when the marker does not take part.

```{r}
#| label: definitions

definitions <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip43_cell_type_definitions.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# The file names detectors, because that is what the score has to match against
# the data. Here the columns are shown as markers, so this table and the scaled
# table below can be read side by side.
detector_to_marker <- c(
  "Comp-APC-A" = "CD19",
  "Comp-BV421-A" = "CD20",
  "Comp-PerCP-Cy5-5-A" = "IgD",
  "Comp-BV786-A" = "CD27",
  "Comp-BUV395-A" = "CD38"
)
shown <- definitions
names(shown)[match(names(detector_to_marker), names(shown))] <- detector_to_marker

kable(
  shown[, c("cell_type", unname(detector_to_marker))],
  caption = "The definitions the labels are scored against. A blank means the marker takes no part in that type."
)
```

The reasoning behind each row is kept in the file itself, in a `note` column left
out of the table above for width.

```{r}
#| label: definition-notes

kable(
  definitions[, c("cell_type", "note")],
  caption = "Why each definition is written that way.",
  col.names = c("Cell type", "Note")
)
```

Five markers do the labelling. The clustering itself used seven, adding
cytoplasmic immunoglobulin and HLA-DR, so the scaled table below carries two
columns that the score does not read. They are shown because they help a reader
judge a label even when the rule ignores them.

**Step 2. Take the median of every marker in every cluster, and scale it.** Each
marker is rescaled to run from 0 to 1 across the fifteen clusters, so a bright
marker and a dim one carry equal weight. The score reads this table and not the
raw medians.

```{r}
#| label: scaled-expression

scaled <- ReadOutput("spleen_cluster_scaled_expression.csv")
kable(
  scaled,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Median expression per cluster, scaled from 0 to 1 within each marker. This is the table the score reads."
)
```

**Step 3. Score every cluster against every definition.** For each marker the
definition names, add the scaled value where it expects `pos`, add twice the
scaled value where it expects `high`, and add one minus the scaled value where it
expects `neg`. Divide by the total weight.

The division matters. An earlier version summed instead, which rewards a
definition for naming more markers rather than for fitting better, and the label
with the longest marker list then wins clusters it has no business winning.

**Step 4. Take the best score, and record how close the second was.** That gap is
the margin, and it is the part of the output that says how much to trust the
label.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-annotation

annotation <- ReadOutput("spleen_cluster_annotation.csv")
kable(
  annotation[, c("cluster", "events", "percent_of_total", "cell_type",
                 "runner_up", "margin", "asc_percent_by_manual_gate")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The fifteen metaclusters, their label, the runner up, and the gap between them.",
  col.names = c("Cluster", "Events", "Percent", "Label", "Runner up", "Margin",
                "ASC percent by the manual gate")
)
```

### Whether the labels are any good

The last two columns check each other, and they were produced without sharing any
information. The label comes from marker expression against a definitions file.
The final column comes from a gate an analyst drew in FlowJo.

Cluster 4 is labelled antibody secreting cells with a margin of 0.409, and the
manual gate calls 91.7 percent of its events ASC. Cluster 3 gets the same label
with a margin of 0.136, and the gate agrees on 60.3 percent. Two independent
routes to the same conclusion.

Read the scaled table for cluster 4 and the label is obvious without any
arithmetic: CD38 at 1.00, CD27 at 1.00, CD20 at 0.02. Highest CD38 in the panel,
CD27 positive, CD20 switched off. That is the paper's definition of an ASC.

Five of the fifteen labels carry a margin below 0.1, and those should be read as
undecided rather than as answers.

Two of them are informative. Cluster 12 has CD19 at 0.93 and CD20 at 0.90 with IgD
at 0.06 and CD27 at 0.12, so it is a B cell that is neither IgD positive nor CD27
positive. Cluster 14 has both IgD at 0.78 and CD27 at 0.64, so it is positive for
both. Neither state is in the definitions file, and the low margins are the method
reporting that rather than hiding it.

Cluster 7 is the one clear error. It is labelled antibody secreting cells and the
manual gate calls 0.7 percent of it ASC. Its margin is 0.045. The label is wrong
and the margin says so.

### What had to be corrected

The first version of the definitions file required memory B cells to be positive
for cytoplasmic immunoglobulin and for HLA-DR. On this panel the FITC channel
carries cytoplasmic Ig, which is high on ASC and low elsewhere, and HLA-DR varies.
Those two requirements pulled the memory B score down far enough that cluster 13,
which is 16.7 percent of the file with CD19 at 0.96, CD20 at 0.77, CD27 at 0.74
and IgD at 0.14, was labelled non-B by a margin of 0.007.

The definitions were cut back to the markers that actually define these subsets:
CD19, CD20, IgD, CD27 and CD38. Cluster 13 is now labelled memory B cells with a
margin of 0.240.

That correction is worth recording rather than quietly applying. The method did
not fail there; the definitions did, and the margin of 0.007 flagged it before
anyone looked at the biology.

Compare the frequency the clustering produces with the manual value. Spleen gives
4.03 percent against 3.34, tonsil 0.77 against 0.86, bone marrow 0.43 against
0.45. Those are within a factor of 1.2. The template was out by a factor of 18.

## Part 5: the phenotype claims

```{r}
#| label: phenotype

phenotype <- ReadOutput("phenotype.csv")
kable(
  phenotype[, c("tissue", "ssc_asc", "ssc_other", "ssc_ratio")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Median side scatter of ASC against the rest of the dumped population.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "ASC", "Other cells", "Ratio")
)
```

The paper warns:

> ASC contain more cytoplasm due to their active production of antibody, and thus
> do not cluster with a typical low-side scatter "lymphocyte" gate.

Reproduced in all four tissues. ASC scatter 1.8 to 2.7 times more light than the
cells around them.

This claim has a direct consequence for automated gating and it is the reason the
template above uses a permissive `boundary` gate on scatter rather than a
`flowClust` lymphocyte gate. A conventional lymphocyte gate would have removed
much of the target population before any marker was looked at, and the analysis
would have run to completion and reported a number.

```{r}
#| label: cd20

kable(
  phenotype[, c("tissue", "cd20_asc", "cd20_other", "cd20_difference")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Median CD20 on ASC against the rest of the dumped population.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "ASC", "Other cells", "Difference")
)
```

> Mature B cells express the phosphoglycoproteins CD19 and CD20, and on
> differentiation to ASCs, CD20 is downregulated.

Reproduced in all four tissues, with the difference running from 7 to 38 units.

```{r}
#| label: tissue-variation

kable(
  phenotype[, c("tissue", "cd19_asc", "hladr_asc", "cd38_asc")],
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Median intensity among ASC only, by tissue.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "CD19", "HLA-DR", "CD38")
)

variation <- ReadOutput("tissue_variation.csv")
kable(
  variation,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Spread of the ASC median across the four tissues.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "CV across tissues, percent")
)
```

> The ratio of CD19+ to CD19- on ASC varies by tissue niche.

CD19 varies across tissues among ASC, from 127 in bone marrow to 165 in tonsil.
The direction matches the literature the paper cites, where CD19 negative ASC are
enriched in bone marrow.

The paper also names Ki67 as varying by tissue. That cannot be tested here,
because the PE channel in these deposited files carries HLA-DR and not Ki67. The
paper describes both as options for that channel. The claim is recorded as not
measurable rather than as failed.

## Part 6: every claim, with a verdict

The sections above measure. This one decides, so that no claim in the file is left
without an answer.

The seven claims live in `gating/omip43_paper_claims.csv`, each with the sentence
it came from, so a reader can check the claim against the paper before checking
the number against the data.

```{r}
#| label: claims-file

claims <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip43_paper_claims.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  claims[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "measure", "test", "figure")],
  caption = "The claims as recorded. The quote column holds the sentence each came from and is left out here for width."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: verdicts

verdicts <- ReadOutput("claims_verdicts.csv")
kable(
  verdicts[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "expected", "observed", "verdict")],
  caption = "Each claim against the deposited data.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "Short name", "Paper expects", "Observed", "Verdict")
)
```

Five of the seven reproduce cleanly. The two that do not are both counting claims,
and neither is a failure of the biology.

Claim 2 fails outright: no replicate falls in the stated 400 to 2,000 range. Claim
3 is met in spleen and tonsil and missed in blood and bone marrow. Both come from
the same sentence, and both track the same thing, which is how rare the cells are
in a given tissue.

One claim could not be tested at all. The paper names Ki67 alongside CD19 and
HLA-DR as varying between tissues, and the PE channel in these deposited files
carries HLA-DR rather than Ki67. The paper describes both as options for that
channel. It is recorded here as not measurable rather than counted as a failure,
because the data to test it was never deposited.

### The same claims, from a population the manual gate never touched

Everything above defines ASC by the gate the authors drew. That asks whether the
paper's conclusions follow from its own analysis, which is worth knowing and is not
the same as reproducing them independently.

So the population was rebuilt from scratch. Each tissue was clustered, and the
clusters carrying the highest median CD38 taken as the population. The manual gate
was not consulted at any point.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-route

cluster_route <- ReadOutput("cluster_route_phenotype.csv")
kable(
  cluster_route[, c("tissue", "asc_clusters", "asc_percent", "manual_percent",
                    "agreement_percent", "ssc_ratio", "cd20_difference")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "ASC defined by clustering alone, against the manual value for the same file.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "Clusters used", "Clustering percent", "Manual percent",
                "Agreement percent", "Side scatter ratio", "CD20 difference")
)
```

All four tissues land close. Bone marrow gives 0.42 percent against 0.45, spleen
2.90 against 3.34, tonsil 0.68 against 0.86, blood 0.49 against 0.33. Agreement on
which individual events are selected runs from 64.5 percent in blood to 95.1
percent in bone marrow.

```{r}
#| label: both-routes

both <- ReadOutput("claims_both_routes.csv")
kable(
  both[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "route", "observed", "verdict")],
  caption = "Each claim by both routes. The two counting claims can only be tested on gated counts, so they appear once.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "Short name", "Route", "Observed", "Verdict")
)
```

Four of the five claims that clustering can test reproduce by clustering, with the
same directions and comparable magnitudes as the authors' own gates. The fifth
fails on a margin of 0.07 percentage points, and the next section explains why that
verdict is kept rather than tuned away.

### Getting there took two attempts, and the first one failed

The first version of this route selected clusters by scoring their whole marker
profile against a definitions file. It worked in tonsil and spleen and failed
badly in bone marrow, calling 9.44 percent of the parent ASC where the manual gate
called 0.45, with only 4.1 percent of the selected events inside that gate.

The numbers said where to look. Precision in bone marrow was 4 to 7 percent while
recall was 87 to 99, so the target cells were being found and then diluted in a
cluster far too large to be ASC. That is not a clustering problem. It is the rule
that decides which cluster to keep.

Forty-eight configurations were then measured across all four tissues, varying the
number of metaclusters, whether scatter channels join the clustering, whether
channels are scaled, and the selection rule. Each was ranked on its worst tissue
rather than its average, because an average hides a total failure.

```{r}
#| label: sweep-by-rule

sweep_summary <- ReadOutput("clustering_sweep_summary.csv")
by_rule <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  c("profile", "cd38 top 1", "cd38 top 2", "cd38 top 3"),
  function(rule) {
    piece <- sweep_summary[sweep_summary$selection == rule, ]
    data.frame(
      selection = rule,
      configurations = nrow(piece),
      best_worst_f1 = max(piece$worst_f1),
      median_worst_f1 = stats::median(piece$worst_f1),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
))
kable(
  by_rule,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The selection rule, summarised over every combination of the other three settings.",
  col.names = c("Selection rule", "Configurations", "Best worst-tissue F1",
                "Median worst-tissue F1")
)
```

The selection rule decides everything and the other three settings barely matter.
Every profile configuration lands between 6.8 and 12.2 on its worst tissue. Every
configuration that ranks on CD38 and takes the top one lands between 48.7 and 77.1.

The reason is in the paper, not in the parameters:

> ASC also express very high levels of the ectoenzyme CD38 and are positive for the
> TNF-family receptor CD27. Very high CD38 expression is in fact considered
> adequate for basic identification of ASC.

The population is defined by one marker being extreme, not by the shape of a
profile. Taking three clusters is worse than taking one, at a best worst-tissue F1
of 10.0, because the third admits a population that is positive without being
extreme.

```{r}
#| label: sweep-top

kable(
  head(sweep_summary, 8),
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The eight best configurations. The chosen one is the first row.",
  col.names = c("Metaclusters", "Scatter", "Scaled", "Selection", "Mean F1",
                "Worst F1", "Worst tissue")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: selection-rule

improvement <- ReadOutput("clustering_improvement.csv")
kable(
  improvement,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The first configuration against the chosen one, scored against the manual gate.",
  col.names = c("Tissue", "First precision", "First recall", "First F1",
                "Chosen precision", "Chosen recall", "Chosen F1")
)
```

Bone marrow goes from the worst tissue to the best, at 95.1 percent agreement.

### The trade-off the sweep exposed

Choosing the top two clusters instead of the top one reproduces all five claims but
agrees less well with the manual gate, at a worst-tissue F1 of 69.6 against 77.1.
Choosing the top one agrees better and loses claim 1.

The report keeps the sweep winner, and claim 1 therefore fails on the clustering
route. It is worth seeing why rather than switching to whichever rule scores
better on the claim table.

Claim 1 says ASC are rarest in blood. By the manual gate that is clear: 0.26
percent in blood against 0.41 in bone marrow. By the clustering route the two are
0.49 and 0.42, so bone marrow comes out marginally lower and the ordering flips.

The two tissues are 0.07 percentage points apart. That gap is smaller than the
difference between the clustering route and the manual gate in either tissue on its
own, so the method cannot resolve it, and a verdict of reproduced would have been
luck rather than evidence.

### What this step is and is not

The manual gate was used to score the configurations above, which makes this a
calibration step rather than an independent test. Choosing a method by how well it
matches a reference is legitimate. Calling the result independent afterwards would
not be.

What survives that objection is the reasoning. The rule was not found by searching
for whatever matched best. It was taken from a sentence in the paper, and the sweep
then confirmed that every rule ignoring that sentence performs six times worse.

```{r}
#| label: verdict-summary

summary_table <- as.data.frame(table(verdicts$verdict))
colnames(summary_table) <- c("verdict", "claims")
kable(summary_table, caption = "The seven claims, summarised.")
```

## Discussion

### The failure is silent, which is the part that matters

The template ran to completion on every tissue. It raised no error, produced a
population, and reported a percentage. Nothing in the output said that the CD38
high gate had kept everything handed to it.

That is the risk in an automated pipeline, and it is worse than a crash. A crash
stops you. A number does not.

The check that caught it here is cheap and general: compare the automated result
against a gate somebody drew by hand, on the same file, before trusting the
pipeline on files nobody has looked at.

### Rarity is what breaks the density method

Part 3b separates two explanations that are easy to confuse.

The first is that CD38 high has no density valley at all. That is not quite true.
In spleen a single `mindensity` cut lands at 144.2 against the analyst's 141.8,
and keeps 3.48 percent of events against their 3.59 percent.

The second is that the population must be abundant enough to leave a feature in
the density curve. That is what the data supports. Spleen holds 3.3 percent ASC and
the method works. Blood, bone marrow and tonsil hold 0.3 to 0.9 percent, and the
cut falls 40 to 60 units too low, keeping 14 to 35 percent of events instead of
about 1 to 3.

So the rule is not that density gating cannot find a bright tail. It is that a
density method needs the population to be common enough to bend the curve, and a
rare cell panel is precisely the case where it is not.

### Why clustering does better here

Clustering never looks for a valley on one axis. It groups events by their
position across all seven markers at once, and ASC differ from their neighbours on
four of them together: CD38 bright, CD27 positive, CD20 low and side scatter high.

That is why the clustering route lands within a factor of 1.5 of the manual value
in all four tissues, including bone marrow at 0.42 percent against 0.45, where the
density gate was out by threefold in the other direction.

The two automated routes therefore do not fail together. The density gate failed
in three tissues of four and the clustering route, once its selection rule matched
the paper's own definition, failed in none.

It took two attempts to get there, and the first attempt failed in bone marrow for
a reason worth carrying forward. A rare population does not claim a cluster of its
own, so the rule that picks which cluster to keep matters more than the clustering
parameters. Across all 48 configurations, every rule that scored the whole
marker profile stayed below an F1 of 12.2 on its worst tissue. Every rule that
ranked on CD38 and took the top cluster reached 48.7 or better.

### What this shows and what it does not

It shows that an automated template can fail silently on a published panel, that
the failure tracks how rare the target population is, and that a different
automated method recovers the same cells without hand tuning.

It does not show that clustering is safe. The selection rule that made it work was
chosen with the manual gate in hand, so this is a calibrated method rather than an
independent one, and blood still agrees on only 64.5 percent of the events it
selects.

It does not measure analyst variation. Seven replicate acquisitions of one tube
are not seven analysts, and the tonsil result where the measured CV fell below the
Poisson floor shows those replicates are not fully independent of one another.

What the arithmetic did show is worth keeping. A measured spread that falls below
the counting floor is a statement about the study design rather than about the
biology, and one line of Poisson arithmetic was enough to see it.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, 2.6 GB of the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/OMIP-43

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/06_omip43_asc_analysis.R

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/omip43_asc_analysis.qmd
```
